blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Reflection: When light rays strike the boundary of two media such as air and glass, a part of light is turned back into the same medium. This is called Reflection of Light.

Laws of Reflection

1. First Law-The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. This plane is called the plane of incidence (or plane of reflection).This condition can be expressed mathematically as

$\hat{e} .(\hat{\mathrm{n}} \times \hat{\mathrm{r}})=0$

2. Second Law- The angle of incidence (the angle between normal and the incident ray) and the angle of reflection (the angle between the reflected ray and the normal) are equal.

$\angle \mathrm{i}=\angle \mathrm{r}$

Object: Light rays incident on an optical element is responsible to define object. Object is defined as the point of intersection of incident rays.

Image: Light rays formed after interaction (either reflection or refraction) with an optical element is responsible to define image. Image is defined as the point of intersection of reflected or refracted rays.

Image formation in plane mirror:

Note: Perpendicular distance of object from plane mirror is equal to perpendicular distance of image from plane mirror.

Characteristics of image due to reflection by a plane mirror:

(1) Distance of object from mirror = Distance of image from the mirror.

(2) All the incident rays from a point object will meet or appear to meet at a single point after reflection from a plane mirror which is called image.

(3) The line joining a point object and its image is normal to the reflecting surface.

Properties of the image of an extended object, formed by a plane mirror:

(1) Size of extended object = Size of extended image.

(2) The image is virtual & erect, if the real extended object is placed parallel to the mirror.

(3) The image is inverted if the extended object lies perpendicular to the plane mirror.

(4) For a real object the image is virtual and for a virtual object the image is real.

Note: The image formed by a plane mirror suffers lateral–inversion, i.e., left is turned into right and vice–versa with respect to object in the image formed by a plane mirror.

Analog clock and plane mirror: When plane mirror is placed in front of the analog clock then the time observed by the observer in image of clock is different from the actual time.

columns: (a) If actual time is in HH : 00 then time observed in the image of clock is,$\begin{array}{r} 12: 00 \\ -\mathrm{HH}: 00 \\ \hline \mathrm{xx}: 00 \end{array}$
(b) If actual time is in HH : MM then time observed in the image of clock is,$\begin{array}{r} 11: 60 \\ -H H: M M \\ \hline x x: y y \end{array}$

(c) If actual time is in HH : MM : SS then time observed in the imageof clock is,$\begin{array}{r} 11: 59: 60 \\ -\mathrm{HH}: \mathrm{MM}: \mathrm{SS} \\ \hline \mathrm{xx}: \mathrm{yy}: \mathrm{zz} \end{array}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing object and image distances: Students often assume the image distance is the same as the object distance but forget that the image is virtual and formed behind the mirror.
  • Using mirror formula incorrectly: Plane mirrors don't require the mirror formula because the focal length is infinite; applying it can lead to confusion.
  • Misunderstanding image characteristics: Students may forget that the image is virtual, upright, and the same size as the object.
  • Incorrect ray diagram construction: Students might incorrectly draw ray diagrams or forget that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Angle of Deviation (ẟ):When light ray is incident on plane mirror then due to reflection its path get deviated, so the angle by which it got deviated is known as angle of deviation.

(1)  For a single reflection  $\delta=\pi-2 i$

The graph between ẟ and i is a straight line with a negative slope.

$\delta=-2 \mathrm{i}+\pi$ Compare the above relation with straight line relation y = mx + c

Note: When light strikes the mirror perpendicularly (normally) then after reflection it retrace its path.

(2) Net angle of deviation after two reflection(When two plane mirrors are inclined at angle  $\theta$ )

When angle of incidence (i) is less then angle between the mirrors ($\theta $) that is { i < $\theta $ }

Then only use this formula :-

$\delta_{\text {net }}=360^{\circ}-2 \theta$

Here, $\delta_{\text {net }}$for two reflection is independent of angle of incidence.

Rotation of plane mirror: If the direction of the incident ray is kept constant and the mirror is rotated through an angle $\theta$ about an axis in the plane of mirror, then the reflected ray rotates through an angle 2 $\theta$ in the same sense.

Rotation of Incident Ray: If the mirror is kept fixed and the incident ray is rotated, then the reflected ray will rotate in the opposite sense by the same angle.

Field of View: The region in which observer‘s eye must be present in order to view the image is called field of view. Observer A will able to see the image because he receive reflected rays but observer B can not see the image.

  • To see the complete image in a plane mirror the minimum length of plane mirror should be half the height of a person.
  • Height of mirror from ground
$y=\frac{\text { Height of eye level from ground }}{2}$

  • This result does not depend on position of eye (height of the eye from ground).
  • This result is independent of the distance of person from the mirror.
Note: If height of eyes is not given in question, then consider the eyes at top of the head and solve the question

modules.name: Velocity of image in Plane Mirror

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Velocity of Image in Plane Mirror :

Case-1: When object is moving perpendicular to the plane mirror:

From mirror property :

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{OM}}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{IM}}$

Differentiate with respect to time,

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{OM}}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{IM}} \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{O}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}=-\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{I}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}\right) \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_I=2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{O}} \end{aligned}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_I=$velocity of image with respect to ground and perpendicular to the plane of mirror

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{o}}=$ velocity of object with respect to ground and perpendicular to the plane of mirror

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}=$velocity of mirror with respect to ground and perpendicular to the plane of mirror

Case-2: When object is moving parallel in front of plane mirror:

When object moves parallel to the plane mirror then the velocity of image is same as velocity of object.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{i}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{o}}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{i}}=$velocity of image with respect to ground and parallel to mirror.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{o}}=$velocity of object with respect to ground and parallel to mirror.

Focal length of a spherical mirror

For marginal rays,

$f=R-\frac{R}{2 \cos i}$

If rays are paraxial then,

$f=\frac{R}{2}$

Image Formation by Spherical Mirror:-

Sign Convention for mirror:-

  • All distances are measured from pole of spherical mirror.
  • Distance measured in the direction of light are taken as positive and opposite to light direction are taken as negative.
  • Distance measured above the principal axis are taken as positive and below the principal axis are taken as negative.
Mirror Formula: Relation between u, v and f in spherical mirror.

$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}$

Note:

• Valid only for paraxial rays.
    • Object distance (u) are negative for real object and positive for virtual object.
    • Image distance (v) are taken as negative for real image and positive for virtual image.

• ${F_{concave\,mirror}} = \,Negative$   and   ${F_{convex\,mirror}} = \,Positive$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
(1) Transverse or Lateral Magnification: If one-dimensional object is placed perpendicular to the principal axis

$m=m_t=\frac{h_i}{h_0}=-\frac{v}{u}=\frac{f}{f-u}=\frac{f-v}{f}$

(2) Longitudinal Magnification: If an object is placed along the principal axis then ratio of length of image and length of object is called longitudinal or axial magnification.

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{L}}=\dfrac{\text { length of image }}{\text { length of object }}=\dfrac{l_{\mathrm{i}}}{l_0}$

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{L}}=\dfrac{\text { length of image }}{\text { length of object }}=\dfrac{\left|\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1\right|}{\left|\mathrm{u}_2-\mathrm{u}_1\right|}$

For small object only: $\displaystyle m_L=\frac{d v}{d u}=-\frac{v^2}{u^2}=-m_T^2$

(3) Superficial Magnification: If two-dimensional object is placed with its plane perpendicular to the principal axis then its magnification is known as superficial magnification.

$\dfrac{A_i}{A_o}=m_t^2=m_s$

Newton’s Formula

$\mathrm{x}_1$ : Object distance from focus

$\mathrm{x}_2$: Image distance from focus

The relation between $\mathrm{x}_1$ , $\mathrm{x}_2$ and f is $\mathrm{f}=\sqrt{\mathrm{x}_1 \mathrm{x}_2}$.

All velocities are instantaneous.

Cutting of mirror:- All the parts of the mirror have the same hollow sphere, so its centre of curvature is same therefore, number of images found is one. The intensity of the image decreases.

modules.name: Refractive Index and Refraction of Light

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Refractive index (μ): The refractive index of the material is an indicator of its optical density.

Optical density $ \uparrow \Rightarrow \mu \uparrow \Rightarrow V \downarrow$

Absolute Refractive Index or simply refractive index of a medium : Absolute Refractive Index or simply refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum (c) to the speed of light in that medium (v).

$\mu=\frac{c}{V} ; \quad \mu \geq 1$

Relative refractive index : When light passes from one medium to another medium

${ }_1 \mu_2=\mu_{21}=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} $ ($ \mu_{21}=$ index of medium-2 with respect to medium-1.)

$\mu_{21}=\frac{1}{\mu_{12}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mu_{21} \times \mu_{12}=1$

Refractive index of water with respect to glass,

$\mu_{w g}=\frac{\mu_w}{\mu_g}=\frac{4 / 3}{3 / 2}=\frac{8}{9}$

Note:

  • The medium with a higher refractive index in which speed of light is comparatively less is known as optically denser medium.
  • The medium with lower refractive index in which the speed of light is comparatively more is known as optically rarer medium.
  • Optical density should not be confused with mass density, which is mass per unit volume. It is possible that mass density of an optically denser medium may be less than that of an optically rarer medium (optical density is the ratio of the speed of light in two media) i.e. both optical density and mass density are different term.
  • Refraction of Light : Refraction is the phenomenon in which ray of light bends when it passes obliquely from one medium (such as air) into another medium (such as glass) in which its velocity is different.
Laws of Refraction :

(1) Incident ray, refracted ray and normal always lie in the same plane.

(2)The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant, for the light of a given colour and for the given pair of media.

$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\mu_{21} \Rightarrow \mu_1 \sin i=\mu_2 \sin r(\text { Snell's Law })$

$\lambda_1 \mu_1=\lambda_2 \mu_2$

$\frac{\sin \mathrm{i}}{\sin \mathrm{r}}=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{v}_2}$

Bending of light ray :

Case(1) : When light rays goes from rarer medium to denser medium.

Light rays bend towards the normal after refraction.

Case(2) : When light rays goes from denser medium to rarer medium.

Light rays bend away from the normal after refraction.

Note: If the light is incident normally then it goes to the second medium without bending, but still it is called refraction.

$\sin \theta_c=\frac{1}{t_2 / 10 t_1}=\frac{10 t_1}{t_2} \Rightarrow \theta_c=\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{10 t_1}{t_2}\right)$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Refraction through Multiple Parallel Slabs :

(a) In place of five parallel slabs, if there are m numbers of parallel slabs, then we can consider the following equation;

$\mu_1 \sin \theta_1=\mu_m \sin \theta_m$

(b) When first and last medium are same then the incident ray and emergent ray are parallel to each other.

Refraction through a single plane surface (Apparent Depth) :

If a point object in denser medium is observed from rare medium and boundary is plane.

$\dfrac{\text { Apparent distance }}{\text { Actual distance }}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{d}}=\dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}$

Velocity of image in plane refraction:

$\vec{V}_{\text{IS}}=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}\vec{V}_{\text{OS}}
$

$ \mathrm{\vec V}_{IS}=$ velocity of image with respect to surface (boundary).

$\vec V_{0 S}=$ velocity of object with respect to surface (boundary).

Refraction through glass slab (Normal Shift) : When an object is placed in front of a transparent slab then it appears for an observer shift (S) as shown in figure. Distance between object and image is S or we can say object appears to shift at a distance S. This distance is called Normal shift.

$\mathrm{S}=\mathrm{t}\left[1-\frac{\mu_{\text {surrounding }}}{\mu_{\text {slab }}}\right]$

$\text { If surrounding medium is air then, } \mu^{\prime}=1$

$\mathrm{S}=\mathrm{t}\left[1-\frac{1}{\mu}\right]$

Refraction Through Glass Slab (Lateral Shift)

Lateral Shift: For a rectangular slab, refraction takes place at two interfaces. It is easily seen from the diagram that the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray-there is no deviation, but it does suffer lateral displacement/shift with respect to the incident ray. The perpendicular distance between incident and emergent ray is known as lateral shift (d).

$\mathrm{d}=\frac{\mathrm{t}}{\cos \mathrm{r}} \sin (\mathrm{i}-\mathrm{r})$

Calculation of time:

Time taken by light ray to cross the slab is.

$\mathrm{T}=\frac{\mu \mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{c} \cos \mathrm{r}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Total Internal Reflection (T.I.R.): When light ray travels from denser to rarer medium, it bends away from the normal. If the angle of incidence is increased, the angle of refraction also increases. At a particular value of angle, the refracted ray subtends 90° angle with the normal, this angle of incidence is known as critical angle $(\theta_{c})$. If angle of incidence increases further, the ray comes back to the same medium. This phenomenon is known as total internal reflection

$\begin{aligned}  & \sin \theta_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{D}}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{D}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{D}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}} \end{aligned}$

Conclusion: For T.I.R. light must travel from Denser medium to Rarer medium (for example, glass to air, water to air, glass to water etc.)

$\mathrm{i}<\theta_{\mathrm{c}} \text { : Refraction }$

$\text { i = } \theta_c \text { : Grazing Emergence (refraction) }$

$i>\theta_c: \operatorname{TIR}$

$\sin \theta_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{D}}}$

If rarer medium is air, $\sin \theta_C=\frac{1}{\mu}$

Circle of illuminance: Ray incident from denser to rarer medium undergoes total internal reflection when their angle of incidence become more than the critical angle, this situation creates a circular region from which light escapes and is called circle of illuminance.

Radius of circular portion, $r=\frac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2-1}}$

blocks.title: Common Confusion
blocks.text:
• Confusing Total Internal Reflection with Regular Reflection
  • Misunderstanding the Critical Angle
  • Not Realising TIR Requires Two Media
  • Confusing the Critical Angle: Misunderstanding or incorrectly calculating the critical angle, especially when TIR does not occur.
  • Sign Errors in Refractive Indices: Confusing the direction of light and incorrectly applying the sign of refractive indices, particularly when transitioning from denser to rarer media.
  • Forgetting TIR Conditions: Overlooking the requirement that TIR occurs only when light travel from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

Application of TIR

1. The sparkling of diamond :- Cutting of diamonds are such that $\mathrm{i}>\theta_c $. So TIR will take place again and again inside it. The light which beams out from a few places in some specific directions makes it sparkle.

2. Mirage and looming :Mirage takes place in hot regions. The light from distant objects appears to be reflected from ground. For mirage to form refractive index goes on increasing as we go up. Looming takes place in cold regions. The light from distant objects appears to be flying. For looming to form refractive index goes on decreasing.

3. Optical Fibre: An optical fibre is a cylindrical dielectric waveguide (nonconducting waveguide) that transmits light along its axis through the process of total internal reflection.

$\sin \mathrm{i}<\sqrt{\mu_1^2-\mu_2^2}$

For maximum value,

$\sin \mathrm{i}=\sqrt{\mu_1^2-\mu_2^2}$

Here $i$  is called maximum acceptance angle.

blocks.text:
Refraction Through Single Curved Surfaces:

$\frac{\mu_2}{\mathrm{v}}-\frac{\mu_1}{\mathrm{u}}=\frac{\mu_2-\mu_1}{\mathrm{R}}$

Important points regarding formula

1. Rays should be paraxial.

2. $\mu_2$ is the medium in which light rays enter after refraction and  $\mu_1$  is the medium in which light rays moves before refraction.

3. v , u & R (what ever is given) should be put along with sign.

Focal length in spherical surface:-

First Focus: The first principal focus is the point on the axis where an object should be placed so that the image is formed at infinity.

$\mathrm{f}_1=\frac{-\mu_1 \mathrm{R}}{\left(\mu_2-\mu_1\right)}$

Second Focus: The second principal focus is the point where parallel rays get focused.

$\mathrm{f}_2=\frac{\mu_2 R}{\left(\mu_2-\mu_1\right)}$

Ratio of Focal lengths:

$\frac{f_1}{f_2}=-\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2} \text { or } \frac{f_1}{\mu_1}+\frac{f_2}{\mu_2}=0$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
LENS: A lens is a portion of a transparent material with two refracting surfaces such that at least one is curved with refractive index of its material being different from that of the surroundings.

Rules for image formation:

• A ray passing through optical centre proceeds without deviation through the lens.

• A ray passing through first focus or directed towards it, becomes parallel to the principal axis after refraction from the lens.

• A ray passing parallel to the principal axis passes or appears to pass through F after refraction through the lens.

Image formation in Concave Lens(Diverging Lence):

Object: Object is placed in between −∞ and optical centre

Image: in between –f and optical centre, virtual, erect, diminished

Diverging lens always forms virtual image for real object.

Lens maker's formula:

$\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\left(\dfrac{\mu_l}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right)\left[\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right] \text { Len's maker formula }$

Lens formula.

$\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{v}}-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{u}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}}$

Important points regarding Lens formula

1. Rays should be paraxial.

2. Lenses should be thin.

3. Medium on both side of the Lens should be same.

4. $\mathrm{R}_1$ is the radius of curvature of that surface on which light rays incident initially and  $\mathrm{R}_2$  is the radius of curvature of that surface on which light rays incident after refraction from the first surface.

5. v, u, $\mathrm{R}_1$, $\mathrm{R}_2$, f (whatever is given in question) should be put along with sign.

Sign Convention:

Note:

(1) For converging Lens (convex Lens in air), focal length is positive.

(2) For diverging Lens (concave Lens in air), focal length is negative.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Special Points: Lens Maker Formula

1. Sun-glasses or goggles: radii of curvature of two surfaces are equal with centres of curvatures on the same side of the lens.

$\begin{aligned} &\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}=\infty \Rightarrow \text { and } \mathrm{P}=0\left(\therefore \mathrm{P}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}\right)\\ &\text { Sun-glasses or goggles have no power. } \end{aligned}$

2. If refractive index of medium < refractive index of lens

$\text { If } \mu_{\mathrm{S}}<\mu_{\mathrm{L}} \text { then } \frac{\mu_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{S}}}>1 \text { or }\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{S}}}-1\right)>0$

Convex lens behaves as a convergent lens. While concave lens behaves as a divergent lens.

3.Refractive index of medium = Refractive index of lens

$\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right) ; \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}=\infty \& \mathrm{P}=0$

$\left(\mu_{\mathrm{S}}=\mu_{\mathrm{L}}\right)$
Lens will behave as a plane transparent plate

4.Refractive index of surrounding medium > Refractive index of lens

$\mu_{\mathrm{S}}>\mu_l \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mu_l}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}<1 \text { and }\left(\dfrac{\mu_l}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right)<0$

Convex lens will behave as a divergent lens and concave lens will behave as a convergent lens. An air bubble in water behaves as a concave lens.

Transverse or Lateral Magnification  $\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}}\right)$

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}}=\dfrac{\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{o}}}=\dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{u}}$

Cutting of lens

Case (1): When we cut the lens perpendicular to the principal axis : If the equiconvex lens is cut into equal parts by a vertical plane, the focal length of each part will be double the initial value but intensity of image will remain unchanged.

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{2(\mu-1)}{\mathrm{R}} \\ & \mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2(\mu-1)} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{2}=\frac{(\mu-1)}{\mathrm{R}} \\ & \mathrm{f}^{\prime}=2 \mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{(\mu-1)} \end{aligned}$

Case (2): When we cut the lens parallel to the principal axis: If an equiconvex lens of focal length f is cut into two identical parts by a horizontal plane AB then the focal length of each part will be equal to that of the initial lens; because $\mu$, $R_1$ and $R_2$ will remain unchanged. Only intensity of image will be reduced.

$\therefore \text { intensity }(\mathrm{I}) \propto(\text { aperture })^2$

Note: Two thin coaxial lenses are placed at a small separation d

(provided incident rays are parallel to the principal axis).

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}_2}-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{f}_1 \mathrm{f}_2} \\ & \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}_1+\mathrm{P}_2-\mathrm{dP}_1 \mathrm{P}_2 \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Velocity of Image in Lens

Case (1): When the object is moving along to principal axis of the Lens.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{IL}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}}^2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~V}}_{\mathrm{OL}}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{IL}}=\text { velocity of image with respect to lens. }$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{OL}}=\text { velocity of object with respect to lens. }$

All velocities are instantaneous.

Case (2) : When the object is moving perpendicular to the principal axis of the Lens.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{IL}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~V}}_{\mathrm{OL}} $

All velocities are instantaneous.

Displacement Method: It is used for determination of focal length of convex lens in laboratory. A thin convex lens of focal length f is placed between an object and a screen fixed at a distance D apart. If D > 4f there are two positions of lens corresponding to which a sharp image of the object is formed on the screen.

Note:

(1) If D > 4f Two position of lens could be found to form the real image of the source on the screen.

(2) If D = 4f One position of lens could be found to form the real image of the source on the screen.

(3) If D < 4f No position of lens could be found to form the real image of the source on the screen.

Conclusion:

$\text { (1) } f=\frac{D^2-d^2}{4 D}$

$\text { (2) } \mathrm{m}_1 \times \mathrm{m}_2=1$

$\text { (3) } h_o=\sqrt{h_1 \times h_2}$

$\text { (4) }\left|\mathrm{m}_1-\mathrm{m}_2\right|=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{f}}$

$\text { (5) } \mathrm{D} \geq 4 \mathrm{f}$

$\text { (6) } \mathrm{f}_{\max }=\frac{\mathrm{D}}{4}$

where, d is the displacement of Lens.

D is the distance between object and screen.

Optical Power (Lens and Mirror): Optical power is the degree to which a lens, mirror, or other optical system converges or diverges light. Optical power also referred to as dioptric power, refractive power, focusing power, or convergence power.

Unit of optical power is diopter$\left(m^{-1}\right)$

Power of any converging optical system is positive.

Example : Convex lens in air, concave mirror.

Power of any diverging optical system is negative.

Example : Concave lens in air, convex mirror.

Optical power of different optical system:

(1) Spherical surface:

$\mathrm{P}=\dfrac{\mu_2-\mu_1}{R}$

(2) Thin lens:

$\begin{aligned} & P=\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\left(\frac{\mu_{\ell}}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right)\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right] \\ & \mathrm{P}=\mu_{\mathrm{S}}\left(\frac{\mu_{\ell}}{\mu_{\mathrm{S}}}-1\right)\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right] \\ & \mathrm{P}=\left(\mu_{\ell}-\mu_{\mathrm{S}}\right)\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right] \end{aligned}$

(3) Spherical Mirror:

$\mathrm{P}=-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}}$

Combination of lenses: Two or more than two lens are placed in contact with each other.

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{P}_1+\mathrm{P}_2$

$\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}_1}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}_2}$

If $P_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is +ve then converging lens is formed.

If $P_{\mathrm{eq}}$  is -ve then diverging lens is formed.

If $P_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is zero then plane surface is formed.

blocks.text:
Optical Prism :

An optical prism is a homogeneous solid transparent medium (such as glass) with flat surfaces that refract light. In prism light ray crosses two plane inclined surfaces. These surfaces are called the 'refracting surfaces' and the  angle between them is called the 'refracting angle' or the 'angle of prism'.

i : angle of incidence. e : angle of emergence.

$\mathrm{r}_1 \& \mathrm{r}_2 $ are angle of refraction

A : apex angle of prism OR prism angle OR refracting angle of prism.

$\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{r}_1+\mathrm{r}_2$

Deviation produced by Prism

$\begin{aligned} & \delta_1=\mathrm{i}-\mathrm{r}_1 \\ & \delta_2=\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{r}_2 \end{aligned}$

$\delta_{\text {net }}=\delta_1+\delta_2$

$\delta_{\text {net }}=(\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{e})-\mathrm{A}$

ẟ v/s I curve for prism

(1) The deviation produced by a prism depends on angle of incidence $ i$, angle of prism $A$, refractive index of material $ μ.$

(2) $\delta$ is first decreasing and then increasing for $\mathrm{i}<\mathrm{e}$ and  $\mathrm{i}>\mathrm{e}$ respectively.

(3) For one $\delta\left(\text { except } \delta_{\min }\right)$  there are two values of angle of incidence. If $\mathrm{i} \text { and } \mathrm{e}$  are interchanged then we get the same value of  $\delta$ because of reversibility principle of light.

(4) There is one and only one angle of incidence for which the angle of deviation is minimum$\text { (when } \mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e} \text { ). }$

(5) Before $\mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e}, \delta$ decreases more rapidly than it increases with $\text { i after } \mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e} \text {. }$ Right hand side part of the graph is more tilted then the left hand side.

Minimum Deviation in Prism

From graph condition of minimum deviation is

$\mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e}$

$\mathrm{r}_1=\mathrm{r}_2=\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}$

Relation between Minimum deviation and Refractive index of prism

$\delta_{\mathrm{m}}=2 \mathrm{i}-\mathrm{A}$

$\dfrac{\mu_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}=\dfrac{\sin \left(\dfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{m}}+\mathrm{A}}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right)}$

Note: For an isosceles / equilateral prism, light goes parallel to the base inside the prism.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
The refracting angle of a prism is A, and the refractive index of the material of the prism is cot(A/2). The angle of minimum deviation is:-

(A) 180° – 2A

(B) 90° – A

(C) 180° + 2A

(D) 180° – 3A
blocks.answer:
Ans. (A)

$\mu=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{m}}+\mathrm{A}}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right)}$

$\because \mu=\cot (\mathrm{A} / 2)$

$\therefore \cot (A / 2)=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{\delta_m+A}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$

$\Rightarrow \cos (A / 2)=\sin \left(\frac{\delta_m+A}{2}\right)$

$\Rightarrow 90^{\circ}-\mathrm{A} / 2=\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{m}}+\mathrm{A}}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \delta_{\mathrm{m}}=180^{\circ}-2 \mathrm{~A}$

blocks.text:
Maximum Deviation

$\text { For } \delta_{\max } \text { either } \mathrm{i}=90^{\circ} \text { or } \mathrm{e}=90^{\circ}$

$\text { Then use } \delta_{\text {net }}=(i+e)-A$

Condition of No emergence

$\begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{r}_2\right)_{\min }>\theta_c \\ & A-r_{1 \max }>\theta_c \\ & \text { When } i_{\max }=90^{\circ} \text { then } r_{1 \text { max }}=\theta_c \\ & \text { So, } A-\theta_c>\theta_c \\ & A>2 \theta_C \end{aligned}$

Condition of Always emergence

$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{r}_2\right)_{\max }<\theta_{\mathrm{c}} \\ & \mathrm{~A}-\mathrm{r}_{1 \min }<\theta_{\mathrm{c}} \end{aligned}\\ &\text { When } \mathrm{i}_{\min }=0^{\circ} \text { then } \mathrm{r}_{1 \mathrm{~min}}=0^{\circ} \end{aligned}$

$\text { So, } A_{\max }=\theta_c$

$\therefore A \leqslant \theta_C$

Conclusion

$\text { 1. if } A \leq \theta_c $ ; then light ray always crosses the prism for any value of i.

$\text { 2. if } \mathrm{A}>2 \theta_c $ ; then light ray never crosses the prism for any value of i.

$\text { 3. if } \theta_c<\mathrm{A} \leq 2 \theta_c $; then light ray may crosses the prism or not depends on angle of incidence.

Thin Prism :For a thin prism, prism angle (A) is very small.

If prism is thin then A is very small & then we assume all angles are very small.

$\frac{\mu_p}{\mu_s}=\frac{\left(\frac{\delta_m+A}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)} \Rightarrow \frac{\mu_p}{\mu_s} \times \frac{A}{2}=\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{m}}+A}{2}$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Visual angle:

Visual angle is the angle, a viewed object or image subtends at the eye. It is also called the object’s angular size.

Nearer the object larger the visual angle then object appears big in size.

Note: Near point (N.P.) of normal eye D = 25cm

Far point (F.P.) of normal eye = ∞

Angular Magnification ‘OR’ Magnifying power

M.P. $=\frac{\text { visual angle of image in the presence of instrument }(\beta)}{\text { maximum visual angle of an object in the absence of instrument }(\alpha)}$

(A) Simple Microscope:

$\displaystyle \tan \alpha \approx \alpha=\frac{h_o}{D}$

(1) A single converging lens (convex lens) of small focal length.

(2) When the object is placed between the focus and the optical centre a virtual, magnified and erect image is formed.

(3) Also known as magnifying glass.

Magnifying power :

$\text { M.P. }=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}=\frac{h_o / u}{h_o / D}$

$\text { M.P. }=\frac{\mathrm{D}}{|\mathrm{u}|}$

Case (1): When image is formed at a distance of least distance of distinct vision from the lens.

$\text { (M.P. })_{\max }=\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{u}_{\min }}=1+\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{f}}$

Case (2): When image formed at infinite distance from the lens.

$(\text { M.P. })_{\min }=\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{u}_{\max }}=\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{f}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Compound microscope : A compound microscope is a laboratory instrument with high magnification power, which is consists of more than one lenses. Compound Microscopes are used for the study of structural details of a cell, tissue, or organ in sections. A compound microscope can magnify the image of a tiny object up to 1000.

The final image is virtual, inverted and magnified.

Magnifying Power : Total magnifying power = Linear magnification of objective lens × angular magnification MP of eye lens

$\text { M.P. }=\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{o}} \times \mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{e}}$

$\text { M.P. }=-\left|\frac{v_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{o}}} \frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{e}}}\right|$

Case (1): When final image formed at least distance of distinct vision.

$M P=\frac{v_0}{u_0}\left[1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right]=\frac{f_0}{\left(f_0+u_0\right)}\left[1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right]=\frac{f_0-v_0}{f_0}\left[1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right]$

$\text { Distance between both the lenses, } L=\mathrm{v}_0+\left|\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}\right|$

Case (2): When final image formed at infinity.

$M P=\frac{v_0}{u_0}\left[\frac{D}{f_e}\right]=\frac{\mathrm{f}_0}{\left(f_0+u_0\right)}\left[\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}}\right]=\frac{\left(\mathrm{f}_0-\mathrm{v}_0\right)}{\mathrm{f}_0}\left[\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}}\right]$

$\text { Distance between both the lenses, } L=\mathrm{V}_0+\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}$

Tube length : The distance L, i.e., the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece (focal length $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}} \text {  }$) is called the tube length of the compound microscope.

Magnifying power of compound microscope when final image formed at infinity.

$\text { M.P. }=m_0 \times m_e$

$\text { M.P. }=-\frac{l}{f_0} \times \frac{D}{f_e}$

blocks.question: A compound microscope has a magnifying power 30X. The focal length of its eye-piece is 5 cm. Assuming the final image formed at the least distance of distinct vision (25cm). Calculate the magnification produced by objective.
blocks.answer:
$\text { Given, M.P. }=-30, \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}=5 \mathrm{~cm}$

M.P. of eyepiece when final image formed at 25 cm away,

$\begin{aligned} &m_e=1+\frac{D}{f_e}=1+\frac{25}{5}=6\\ &\text { Now, M.P. }=\mathrm{m}_o \times \mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{e}}\\ &-30=m_o \times 6 \Rightarrow m_o=-5 \end{aligned}$

blocks.question: An angular magnification of 30X is desired using an objective of focal length 1.25 cm and an eye piece of focal length 5 cm. What distance will you set between Objective and Eye piece of the compound microscope for final image at infinity?
blocks.answer:
$\text { Given, M.P. }=-30, \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}}=1.25 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}=5 \mathrm{~cm}$

$\text { If final image at } \infty \text { then } \mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{e}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}}=\dfrac{25}{5}=5$

$\begin{aligned} & \text { M.P. }=m_o \times m_e \\ & -30=m_0 \times 5 \Rightarrow m_0=-6 \\ & m_0=\frac{f_o-V_o}{f_o}=-6 \Rightarrow \frac{1.25-V_o}{1.25}=-6 \Rightarrow V_o=8.75 \mathrm{~cm} \end{aligned}$

$\text { Distance between objective and eyepiece is, } L=V_o+f_e=8.75+5=13.75 \mathrm{~cm}$

blocks.text:
Focal Plane : When light rays are parallel and paraxial but not parallel to principal axis can incident on the lens then the plane where they meet or appears to meet after refraction is known as focal plane.

$\alpha=\frac{h}{f} \Rightarrow h=f \alpha$

Astronomical telescope : The telescope is used to provide angular magnification of distant objects . It also has an objective and an eyepiece. But here, the objective has a large focal length and a much larger aperture than the eyepiece. Light from a distant object enters the objective and a real image is formed in the tube at its second focal point. The eyepiece magnifies this image producing a final inverted image.

Magnifying Power:

$\mathrm{MP}=\frac{\text { visual angle with instrument }(\beta)}{\text { visual angle for unaided eye }(\alpha)} \Rightarrow \mathrm{MP}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{h}}{-\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}}}{\frac{\mathrm{~h}}{\mathrm{f}_0}}=-\frac{\mathrm{f}_0}{\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}} \quad \mathrm{MP}=-\frac{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}}$

Case (1): When final image formed at least distance of distinct vision

$\text { So } M P=-\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_o}{\mathbf{u}_e}=-\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathbf{f}_e}\left[\mathbf{1}+\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_e}{\mathrm{D}}\right]$

$\text { Length of the tube is, } L=f_0+\left|u_e\right|$

Case (2): When final image formed at infinity

$\mathrm{MP}=-\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{e}}}$

$\text { Length of the tube, } L=f_0+f_e$

Cassegrain telescope (Reflecting Telescope) :

• Reflecting Telescopes: Instead of lenses, modern telescopes use concave mirrors to avoid chromatic aberration.
    • Heavy Lenses: Large lenses are difficult to make, support, and are prone to chromatic aberration.
    • Mirror Advantages: Mirrors are lighter, easier to support (can be supported over the entire back), and cheaper to manufacture.
    • Focus Issue: In reflecting telescopes, the objective mirror focuses light inside the tube.
• Cassegrain Design: A convex secondary mirror redirects light through a hole in the primary mirror, resulting in a compact telescope with a long focal length.

blocks.text:
Velocity of Image in Plane Mirror :

Case-1: When object is moving perpendicular to the plane mirror:

From mirror property :

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{OM}}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{x}}_{\mathrm{IM}}$

Differentiate with respect to time,

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{OM}}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{IM}} \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{O}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}=-\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{I}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}\right) \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_I=2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{O}} \end{aligned}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_I=$velocity of image with respect to ground and perpendicular to the plane of mirror

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{o}}=$ velocity of object with respect to ground and perpendicular to the plane of mirror

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{M}}=$velocity of mirror with respect to ground and perpendicular to the plane of mirror

Case-2: When object is moving parallel in front of plane mirror:

When object moves parallel to the plane mirror then the velocity of image is same as velocity of object.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{i}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{o}}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{i}}=$velocity of image with respect to ground and parallel to mirror.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{o}}=$velocity of object with respect to ground and parallel to mirror.

Number of images when mirrors are inclined to each other

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
(1) Transverse or Lateral Magnification: If one-dimensional object is placed perpendicular to the principal axis

$m=m_t=\frac{h_i}{h_0}=-\frac{v}{u}=\frac{f}{f-u}=\frac{f-v}{f}$

(2) Longitudinal Magnification: If an object is placed along the principal axis then ratio of length of image and length of object is called longitudinal or axial magnification.

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{L}}=\dfrac{\text { length of image }}{\text { length of object }}=\dfrac{l_{\mathrm{i}}}{l_0}$

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{L}}=\dfrac{\text { length of image }}{\text { length of object }}=\dfrac{\left|\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1\right|}{\left|\mathrm{u}_2-\mathrm{u}_1\right|}$

For small object only: $\displaystyle m_L=\frac{d v}{d u}=-\frac{v^2}{u^2}=-m_T^2$

(3) Superficial Magnification: If two-dimensional object is placed with its plane perpendicular to the principal axis then its magnification is known as superficial magnification.

$\dfrac{A_i}{A_o}=m_t^2=m_s$

Newton’s Formula

$\mathrm{x}_1$ : Object distance from focus

$\mathrm{x}_2$: Image distance from focus

The relation between $\mathrm{x}_1$ , $\mathrm{x}_2$ and f is $\mathrm{f}=\sqrt{\mathrm{x}_1 \mathrm{x}_2}$.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Refractive index (μ): The refractive index of the material is an indicator of its optical density.

Optical density $ \uparrow \Rightarrow \mu \uparrow \Rightarrow V \downarrow$

Absolute Refractive Index or simply refractive index of a medium : Absolute Refractive Index or simply refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum (c) to the speed of light in that medium (v).

$\mu=\frac{c}{V} ; \quad \mu \geq 1$

Relative refractive index : When light passes from one medium to another medium

${ }_1 \mu_2=\mu_{21}=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} $ ($ \mu_{21}=$ index of medium-2 with respect to medium-1.)

$\mu_{21}=\frac{1}{\mu_{12}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mu_{21} \times \mu_{12}=1$

Refractive index of water with respect to glass,

$\mu_{w g}=\frac{\mu_w}{\mu_g}=\frac{4 / 3}{3 / 2}=\frac{8}{9}$

Note:

  • The medium with a higher refractive index in which speed of light is comparatively less is known as optically denser medium.
  • The medium with lower refractive index in which the speed of light is comparatively more is known as optically rarer medium.
  • Optical density should not be confused with mass density, which is mass per unit volume. It is possible that mass density of an optically denser medium may be less than that of an optically rarer medium (optical density is the ratio of the speed of light in two media) i.e. both optical density and mass density are different term.
  • Refraction of Light : Refraction is the phenomenon in which ray of light bends when it passes obliquely from one medium (such as air) into another medium (such as glass) in which its velocity is different.
Laws of Refraction :

(1) Incident ray, refracted ray and normal always lie in the same plane.

(2)The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant, for the light of a given colour and for the given pair of media.

$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\mu_{21} \Rightarrow \mu_1 \sin i=\mu_2 \sin r(\text { Snell's Law })$

$\lambda_1 \mu_1=\lambda_2 \mu_2$

$\frac{\sin \mathrm{i}}{\sin \mathrm{r}}=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{v}_2}$

Bending of light ray :

Case(1) : When light rays goes from rarer medium to denser medium.

Light rays bend towards the normal after refraction.

Case(2) : When light rays goes from denser medium to rarer medium.

Light rays bend away from the normal after refraction.

Note: If the light is incident normally then it goes to the second medium without bending, but still it is called refraction.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Refraction through Multiple Parallel Slabs :

(a) In place of five parallel slabs, if there are m numbers of parallel slabs, then we can consider the following equation;

$\mu_1 \sin \theta_1=\mu_m \sin \theta_m$

(b) When first and last medium are same then the incident ray and emergent ray are parallel to each other.

Refraction through a single plane surface (Apparent Depth) :

If a point object in denser medium is observed from rare medium and boundary is plane.

$\dfrac{\text { Apparent distance }}{\text { Actual distance }}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{d}}=\dfrac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}$

Velocity of image in plane refraction:

$\vec{V}_{\text{IS}}=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}\vec{V}_{\text{OS}}
$

$ \mathrm{\vec V}_{IS}=$ velocity of image with respect to surface (boundary).

$\vec V_{0 S}=$ velocity of object with respect to surface (boundary).

Refraction through glass slab (Normal Shift) : When an object is placed in front of a transparent slab then it appears for an observer shift (S) as shown in figure. Distance between object and image is S or we can say object appears to shift at a distance S. This distance is called Normal shift.

$\mathrm{S}=\mathrm{t}\left[1-\frac{\mu_{\text {surrounding }}}{\mu_{\text {slab }}}\right]$

$\text { If surrounding medium is air then, } \mu^{\prime}=1$

$\mathrm{S}=\mathrm{t}\left[1-\frac{1}{\mu}\right]$

Refraction Through Glass Slab (Lateral Shift)

Lateral Shift: For a rectangular slab, refraction takes place at two interfaces. It is easily seen from the diagram that the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray-there is no deviation, but it does suffer lateral displacement/shift with respect to the incident ray. The perpendicular distance between incident and emergent ray is known as lateral shift (d).

$\mathrm{d}=\frac{\mathrm{t}}{\cos \mathrm{r}} \sin (\mathrm{i}-\mathrm{r})$

Calculation of time:

Time taken by light ray to cross the slab is.

$\mathrm{T}=\frac{\mu \mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{c} \cos \mathrm{r}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Total Internal Reflection (T.I.R.): When light ray travels from denser to rarer medium, it bends away from the normal. If the angle of incidence is increased, the angle of refraction also increases. At a particular value of angle, the refracted ray subtends 90° angle with the normal, this angle of incidence is known as critical angle $(\theta_{c})$. If angle of incidence increases further, the ray comes back to the same medium. This phenomenon is known as total internal reflection

$\begin{aligned}  & \sin \theta_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{D}}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{D}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{R}}}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{D}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}} \end{aligned}$

Conclusion: For T.I.R. light must travel from Denser medium to Rarer medium (for example, glass to air, water to air, glass to water etc.)

$\mathrm{i}<\theta_{\mathrm{c}} \text { : Refraction }$

$\text { i = } \theta_c \text { : Grazing Emergence (refraction) }$

$i>\theta_c: \operatorname{TIR}$

$\sin \theta_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{R}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{D}}}$

If rarer medium is air, $\sin \theta_C=\frac{1}{\mu}$

Circle of illuminance: Ray incident from denser to rarer medium undergoes total internal reflection when their angle of incidence become more than the critical angle, this situation creates a circular region from which light escapes and is called circle of illuminance.

Radius of circular portion, $r=\frac{h}{\sqrt{\mu^2-1}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Refraction Through Single Curved Surfaces:

$\frac{\mu_2}{\mathrm{v}}-\frac{\mu_1}{\mathrm{u}}=\frac{\mu_2-\mu_1}{\mathrm{R}}$

Important points regarding formula

1. Rays should be paraxial.

2. $\mu_2$ is the medium in which light rays enter after refraction and  $\mu_1$  is the medium in which light rays moves before refraction.

3. v , u & R (what ever is given) should be put along with sign.

Focal length in spherical surface:-

First Focus: The first principal focus is the point on the axis where an object should be placed so that the image is formed at infinity.

$\mathrm{f}_1=\frac{-\mu_1 \mathrm{R}}{\left(\mu_2-\mu_1\right)}$

Second Focus: The second principal focus is the point where parallel rays get focused.

$\mathrm{f}_2=\frac{\mu_2 R}{\left(\mu_2-\mu_1\right)}$

Ratio of Focal lengths:

$\frac{f_1}{f_2}=-\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2} \text { or } \frac{f_1}{\mu_1}+\frac{f_2}{\mu_2}=0$

blocks.title: Core Concepts

Special Points: Lens Maker Formula

1. Sun-glasses or goggles: radii of curvature of two surfaces are equal with centres of curvatures on the same side of the lens.

$\begin{aligned} &\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}=\infty \Rightarrow \text { and } \mathrm{P}=0\left(\therefore \mathrm{P}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}\right)\\ &\text { Sun-glasses or goggles have no power. } \end{aligned}$

2. If refractive index of medium < refractive index of lens

$\text { If } \mu_{\mathrm{S}}<\mu_{\mathrm{L}} \text { then } \frac{\mu_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{S}}}>1 \text { or }\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{S}}}-1\right)>0$

Convex lens behaves as a convergent lens. While concave lens behaves as a divergent lens.

3.Refractive index of medium = Refractive index of lens

$\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right) ; \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}=\infty \& \mathrm{P}=0$

$\left(\mu_{\mathrm{S}}=\mu_{\mathrm{L}}\right)$
Lens will behave as a plane transparent plate

4.Refractive index of surrounding medium > Refractive index of lens

$\mu_{\mathrm{S}}>\mu_l \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mu_l}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}<1 \text { and }\left(\dfrac{\mu_l}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right)<0$

Convex lens will behave as a divergent lens and concave lens will behave as a convergent lens. An air bubble in water behaves as a concave lens.

Transverse or Lateral Magnification  $\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}}\right)$

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}}=\dfrac{\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{o}}}=\dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{u}}$

Cutting of lens

Case (1): When we cut the lens perpendicular to the principal axis : If the equiconvex lens is cut into equal parts by a vertical plane, the focal length of each part will be double the initial value but intensity of image will remain unchanged.

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{2(\mu-1)}{\mathrm{R}} \\ & \mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2(\mu-1)} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{2}=\frac{(\mu-1)}{\mathrm{R}} \\ & \mathrm{f}^{\prime}=2 \mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{(\mu-1)} \end{aligned}$

Case (2): When we cut the lens parallel to the principal axis: If an equiconvex lens of focal length f is cut into two identical parts by a horizontal plane AB then the focal length of each part will be equal to that of the initial lens; because $\mu$, $R_1$ and $R_2$ will remain unchanged. Only intensity of image will be reduced.

$\therefore \text { intensity }(\mathrm{I}) \propto(\text { aperture })^2$

Note: Two thin coaxial lenses are placed at a small separation d

(provided incident rays are parallel to the principal axis).

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}_2}-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{f}_1 \mathrm{f}_2} \\ & \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}_1+\mathrm{P}_2-\mathrm{dP}_1 \mathrm{P}_2 \end{aligned}$

Velocity of Image in Lens

Case (1): When the object is moving along to principal axis of the Lens.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{IL}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}}^2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~V}}_{\mathrm{OL}}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{IL}}=\text { velocity of image with respect to lens. }$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{OL}}=\text { velocity of object with respect to lens. }$

All velocities are instantaneous.

Case (2) : When the object is moving perpendicular to the principal axis of the Lens.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{IL}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{t}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~V}}_{\mathrm{OL}} $

All velocities are instantaneous.

Displacement Method: It is used for determination of focal length of convex lens in laboratory. A thin convex lens of focal length f is placed between an object and a screen fixed at a distance D apart. If D > 4f there are two positions of lens corresponding to which a sharp image of the object is formed on the screen.

Note:

(1) If D > 4f Two position of lens could be found to form the real image of the source on the screen.

(2) If D = 4f One position of lens could be found to form the real image of the source on the screen.

(3) If D < 4f No position of lens could be found to form the real image of the source on the screen.

Conclusion:

$\text { (1) } f=\frac{D^2-d^2}{4 D}$

$\text { (2) } \mathrm{m}_1 \times \mathrm{m}_2=1$

$\text { (3) } h_o=\sqrt{h_1 \times h_2}$

$\text { (4) }\left|\mathrm{m}_1-\mathrm{m}_2\right|=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{f}}$

$\text { (5) } \mathrm{D} \geq 4 \mathrm{f}$

$\text { (6) } \mathrm{f}_{\max }=\frac{\mathrm{D}}{4}$

where, d is the displacement of Lens.

D is the distance between object and screen.

Optical Power (Lens and Mirror): Optical power is the degree to which a lens, mirror, or other optical system converges or diverges light. Optical power also referred to as dioptric power, refractive power, focusing power, or convergence power.

Unit of optical power is diopter$\left(m^{-1}\right)$

Power of any converging optical system is positive.

Example : Convex lens in air, concave mirror.

Power of any diverging optical system is negative.

Example : Concave lens in air, convex mirror.

Optical power of different optical system:

(1) Spherical surface:

$\mathrm{P}=\dfrac{\mu_2-\mu_1}{R}$

(2) Thin lens:

$\begin{aligned} & P=\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=\left(\frac{\mu_{\ell}}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right)\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right] \\ & \mathrm{P}=\mu_{\mathrm{S}}\left(\frac{\mu_{\ell}}{\mu_{\mathrm{S}}}-1\right)\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right] \\ & \mathrm{P}=\left(\mu_{\ell}-\mu_{\mathrm{S}}\right)\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right] \end{aligned}$

(3) Spherical Mirror:

$\mathrm{P}=-\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}}$

Combination of lenses: Two or more than two lens are placed in contact with each other.

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\mathrm{P}_1+\mathrm{P}_2$

$\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}_1}+\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}_2}$

If $P_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is +ve then converging lens is formed.

If $P_{\mathrm{eq}}$  is -ve then diverging lens is formed.

If $P_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is zero then plane surface is formed.

Optical Prism :

An optical prism is a homogeneous solid transparent medium (such as glass) with flat surfaces that refract light. In prism light ray crosses two plane inclined surfaces. These surfaces are called the 'refracting surfaces' and the  angle between them is called the 'refracting angle' or the 'angle of prism'.

i : angle of incidence. e : angle of emergence.

$\mathrm{r}_1 \& \mathrm{r}_2 $ are angle of refraction

A : apex angle of prism OR prism angle OR refracting angle of prism.

$\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{r}_1+\mathrm{r}_2$

Deviation produced by Prism

$\begin{aligned} & \delta_1=\mathrm{i}-\mathrm{r}_1 \\ & \delta_2=\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{r}_2 \end{aligned}$

$\delta_{\text {net }}=\delta_1+\delta_2$

$\delta_{\text {net }}=(\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{e})-\mathrm{A}$

ẟ v/s I curve for prism

(1) The deviation produced by a prism depends on angle of incidence $ i$, angle of prism $A$, refractive index of material $ μ.$

(2) $\delta$ is first decreasing and then increasing for $\mathrm{i}<\mathrm{e}$ and  $\mathrm{i}>\mathrm{e}$ respectively.

(3) For one $\delta\left(\text { except } \delta_{\min }\right)$  there are two values of angle of incidence. If $\mathrm{i} \text { and } \mathrm{e}$  are interchanged then we get the same value of  $\delta$ because of reversibility principle of light.

(4) There is one and only one angle of incidence for which the angle of deviation is minimum$\text { (when } \mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e} \text { ). }$

(5) Before $\mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e}, \delta$ decreases more rapidly than it increases with $\text { i after } \mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e} \text {. }$ Right hand side part of the graph is more tilted then the left hand side.

Minimum Deviation in Prism

From graph condition of minimum deviation is

$\mathrm{i}=\mathrm{e}$

$\mathrm{r}_1=\mathrm{r}_2=\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}$

Relation between Minimum deviation and Refractive index of prism

$\delta_{\mathrm{m}}=2 \mathrm{i}-\mathrm{A}$

$\dfrac{\mu_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}=\dfrac{\sin \left(\dfrac{\delta_{\mathrm{m}}+\mathrm{A}}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right)}$

Note: For an isosceles / equilateral prism, light goes parallel to the base inside the prism.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Maximum Deviation

$\text { For } \delta_{\max } \text { either } \mathrm{i}=90^{\circ} \text { or } \mathrm{e}=90^{\circ}$

$\text { Then use } \delta_{\text {net }}=(i+e)-A$

Condition of No emergence

$\begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{r}_2\right)_{\min }>\theta_c \\ & A-r_{1 \max }>\theta_c \\ & \text { When } i_{\max }=90^{\circ} \text { then } r_{1 \text { max }}=\theta_c \\ & \text { So, } A-\theta_c>\theta_c \\ & A>2 \theta_C \end{aligned}$

Condition of Always emergence

$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{r}_2\right)_{\max }<\theta_{\mathrm{c}} \\ & \mathrm{~A}-\mathrm{r}_{1 \min }<\theta_{\mathrm{c}} \end{aligned}\\ &\text { When } \mathrm{i}_{\min }=0^{\circ} \text { then } \mathrm{r}_{1 \mathrm{~min}}=0^{\circ} \end{aligned}$

$\text { So, } A_{\max }=\theta_c$

$\therefore A \leqslant \theta_C$

Conclusion

$\text { 1. if } A \leq \theta_c $ ; then light ray always crosses the prism for any value of i.

$\text { 2. if } \mathrm{A}>2 \theta_c $ ; then light ray never crosses the prism for any value of i.

$\text { 3. if } \theta_c<\mathrm{A} \leq 2 \theta_c $; then light ray may crosses the prism or not depends on angle of incidence.

Thin Prism :For a thin prism, prism angle (A) is very small.

$\text { In general } \mathrm{A}<10^{\circ}$

If prism is thin then A is very small & then we assume all angles are very small.

$\frac{\mu_p}{\mu_s}=\frac{\left(\frac{\delta_m+A}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)} \Rightarrow \frac{\mu_p}{\mu_s} \times \frac{A}{2}=\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{m}}+A}{2}$

$\delta_{\mathrm{m}}=\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}}-1\right) \mathrm{A}$

The deviation for a small angled prism is independent of the angle of incidence.

blocks.text:
Compound microscope : A compound microscope is a laboratory instrument with high magnification power, which is consists of more than one lenses. Compound Microscopes are used for the study of structural details of a cell, tissue, or organ in sections. A compound microscope can magnify the image of a tiny object up to 1000.

The final image is virtual, inverted and magnified.

Magnifying Power : Total magnifying power = Linear magnification of objective lens × angular magnification MP of eye lens

$\text { M.P. }=\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{o}} \times \mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{e}}$

$\text { M.P. }=-\left|\frac{v_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{o}}} \frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{e}}}\right|$

Case (1): When final image formed at least distance of distinct vision.

$M P=\frac{v_0}{u_0}\left[1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right]=\frac{f_0}{\left(f_0+u_0\right)}\left[1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right]=\frac{f_0-v_0}{f_0}\left[1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right]$

$\text { Distance between both the lenses, } L=\mathrm{v}_0+\left|\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}\right|$

Case (2): When final image formed at infinity.

$M P=\frac{v_0}{u_0}\left[\frac{D}{f_e}\right]=\frac{\mathrm{f}_0}{\left(f_0+u_0\right)}\left[\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}}\right]=\frac{\left(\mathrm{f}_0-\mathrm{v}_0\right)}{\mathrm{f}_0}\left[\frac{\mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}}\right]$

$\text { Distance between both the lenses, } L=\mathrm{V}_0+\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}$

Tube length : The distance L, i.e., the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece (focal length $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}} \text {  }$) is called the tube length of the compound microscope.

Magnifying power of compound microscope when final image formed at infinity.

$\text { M.P. }=m_0 \times m_e$

$\text { M.P. }=-\frac{l}{f_0} \times \frac{D}{f_e}$

blocks.text:
Focal Plane : When light rays are parallel and paraxial but not parallel to principal axis can incident on the lens then the plane where they meet or appears to meet after refraction is known as focal plane.

$\alpha=\frac{h}{f} \Rightarrow h=f \alpha$

Astronomical telescope : The telescope is used to provide angular magnification of distant objects . It also has an objective and an eyepiece. But here, the objective has a large focal length and a much larger aperture than the eyepiece. Light from a distant object enters the objective and a real image is formed in the tube at its second focal point. The eyepiece magnifies this image producing a final inverted image.

Magnifying Power:

$\mathrm{MP}=\frac{\text { visual angle with instrument }(\beta)}{\text { visual angle for unaided eye }(\alpha)} \Rightarrow \mathrm{MP}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{h}}{-\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}}}{\frac{\mathrm{~h}}{\mathrm{f}_0}}=-\frac{\mathrm{f}_0}{\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}} \quad \mathrm{MP}=-\frac{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{e}}}$

Case (1): When final image formed at least distance of distinct vision

$\text { So } M P=-\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_o}{\mathbf{u}_e}=-\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathbf{f}_e}\left[\mathbf{1}+\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_e}{\mathrm{D}}\right]$

$\text { Length of the tube is, } L=f_0+\left|u_e\right|$

Case (2): When final image formed at infinity

$\mathrm{MP}=-\dfrac{\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{e}}}$

$\text { Length of the tube, } L=f_0+f_e$

Cassegrain telescope (Reflecting Telescope) :

• Reflecting Telescopes: Instead of lenses, modern telescopes use concave mirrors to avoid chromatic aberration.
    • Heavy Lenses: Large lenses are difficult to make, support, and are prone to chromatic aberration.
    • Mirror Advantages: Mirrors are lighter, easier to support (can be supported over the entire back), and cheaper to manufacture.
    • Focus Issue: In reflecting telescopes, the objective mirror focuses light inside the tube.
• Cassegrain Design: A convex secondary mirror redirects light through a hole in the primary mirror, resulting in a compact telescope with a long focal length.
